articles.title: “反向博弈论”如何控制AI智能体
articles.originalTitle: How “reverse game theory” could keep AI agents in check
articles.summary: 这条新闻与智能体、安全相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：MIT Technology Review：智能体、安全相关动态
articles.fullContent: 一种被称为“反向博弈论”的新方法旨在通过设计激励他们遵守规则的系统来控制强大的人工智能模型。随着人工智能模型变得越来越强大，安全研究人员正在争先恐后地确保它们与人类的欲望“保持一致” --换句话说，确保流氓特工不会违法、入侵未经授权的服务器或向主要城市释放毒气并杀死我们所有人。 到目前为止，这项工作主要集中在试图窥视人工智能的“大脑” ，以了解它在“思考”什么，或者训练模型来塑造我们所珍视的价值观。例如，克劳德就有自己的宪法--一种道德准则。问题是，这些技术似乎并不特别有效：模型已被证明在测试中故意表现不佳，隐藏他们的意图，并误导他们的评估者。 现在，一些对齐研究人员认为，反向博弈论，也称为机制设计，可能会得到更好的结果。博弈论试图预测理性行为者在给定一组特定规则时将如何行为，反向博弈论试图设计规则，以引出我们想要鼓励的行为类型。 现实世界中的机制设计的一个例子可能是将一块蛋糕分成两块的经典策略：一个人切蛋糕，另一个人获得第一选择。这激励刀具尽可能均匀地制造零件。 其他例子包括网约车应用程序中的溢价（鼓励司机在繁忙时段提供服务）和二级价格拍卖（中标者支付第二高出价而不是最高出价的价格）。平台使用这些拍卖来销售在线广告，因为它们鼓励买家出价接近他们愿意支付的最高价格。 在人工智能中，机制设计始于一个前提，即我们可能永远无法充分了解前沿模型的内部运作，以确保它们是一致的。这意味着我们应该设计激励代理以我们想要的方式行事的机制，无论引擎盖下到底发生了什么。 麻省理工学院经济学家斯蒂芬·莫里斯（ Stephen Morris ）以及耶鲁大学和哥伦比亚大学的同事最近的一篇预印本论文提出了一些潜在的机制，可以阻止代理人进行“沙袋”测试（假装比实际情况更糟糕-例如，避免触发安全机制）。而不是仅仅因为它在测试中的表现而获得奖励，一个模型可以因为它的答案预测第二个模型会说什么而获得奖励。 故意装傻变成了失败的赌注。“人工智能代理非常了解其他人工智能代理可以实现的目标，”莫里斯说。“因此，这种交叉检查似乎可以更切实地发挥作用。

articles.rawFullText: A new approach known as “reverse game theory” aims to control powerful AI models by designing systems that incentivize them to stick to the rules. As AI models become more capable, safety researchers are scrambling to ensure they are “aligned” with human desires—to make sure, in other words, that rogue agents don’t break the law, hack into unauthorized servers, or release poison gas into major cities and kill us all. Until now, this work has mostly focused on trying to peer into an AI’s “brain” to understand what it is “thinking,” or training models to hew to values that we hold dear. Claude, for instance, has its constitution —a sort of moral code. The trouble is, these techniques don’t seem to work particularly well: Models have been shown to deliberately underperform on tests, hide their intentions , and mislead their evaluators .  Now some alignment researchers believe that reverse game theory, also known as mechanism design, might get better results. Where game theory tries to predict how rational actors will behave when given a particular set of rules, reverse game theory attempts to design rules that will elicit the kinds of behavior we want to encourage. An example of mechanism design in the real world might be the classic strategy for splitting a piece of cake in two: One person cuts the cake and the other gets the first choice of pieces. This incentivizes the cutter to make the pieces as even as possible. Other examples include surge pricing in ride-hailing apps, which encourages drivers to be available at busy times, and second-price auctions, where the winning bidder pays the price of the second-highest bid instead of the highest. Platforms use these auctions to sell online advertising because they encourage buyers to bid close to the maximum they are willing to pay. In AI, mechanism design starts from the premise that we may never be able to understand enough about the internal workings of frontier models to make sure they are aligned. This means we should design mechanisms that incentivize agents to behave in ways that we want, regardless of what’s actually going on under the hood.  A recent preprint paper by Stephen Morris, an economist at MIT, along with colleagues from Yale and Columbia suggested some potential mechanisms that could stop agents from “sandbagging” tests (pretending to be worse than they actually are—for example, to avoid triggering safety mechanisms).  Instead of being rewarded only for how well it does on a test, a model could be rewarded for how well its answers predict what a second model will say. Deliberately playing dumb becomes a losing bet. “AI agents have a very good understanding of what other AI agents can achieve,” Morris says. “So it does seem like a context where this cross-checking could work more practically.  The paper also suggests pitting agents against each other, creating a competitive dynamic that incentivizes them to perform their best, or pairing agents that are known to be biased in opposite directions and rewarding them depending on how closely their outputs match, thus incentivizing them to reach an optimal answer.  A second approach, as envisioned by Elad Hazan, a professor of computer science at Princeton, is to design mechanisms that take inspiration from the ways human society keeps people “aligned”: social norms, the justice system, the monetary incentives of free-market capitalism. “We want to align superintelligent AI,” he says. “Why don’t we first talk about humans? How do we align humans?” Hazan’s suggested mechanism involves having AI models take turns as either “solvers” that tackle problems or “auditors” that check the others’ work. “One agent acts like law enforcement; the other agent acts like the citizen,” he says.  During training, the models are rewarded depending on outcomes: Solvers that get caught cheating are punished, but so are auditors that fail to catch the cheaters. In situations where there’s a disagreement between auditors and solvers, the case can be sent to “trial”—perhaps a human expert will decide who is right.  There is, Hazan admits, a risk that agents will collude with each other—as auditors have colluded with the businesses they’re meant to be auditing, or corrupt police officers have colluded with criminals. But that problem can be solved by rewarding the auditors well enough, so that being caught isn’t worth the risk (a lot easier in the world of AI training than the real one, where money for police salaries is tight), and by auditing the auditors using techniques akin to employing mystery shoppers.  Hazan points to Nobel Prize–winning work by the economist Gary Becker, who introduced the idea of the “rational offender” in the 1960s. Criminals don’t break the law because they’re inherently bad people, he said. Instead, they do it when it’s the most rational choice given the incentives on offer. Crime makes sense only when the proceeds outweigh the potential punishment.  Alignment shouldn’t be thought of as a property of a model, he argues, but as a descriptor of its behavior at a particular moment. “You are, like, a nice person,” he says. “Are you aligned? I don’t know. Probably you are aligned most of the time, but there could be a situation where you’re not.” One potential issue with applying mechanism design to AI: It relies on the assumption that AI agents behave rationally. Mechanism design has a mixed record with humans, who often fail to behave the way economic models say they should.  It’s ironic: Economists have spent decades trying to reduce human behavior to mathematics, and now, in large language models, we’ve built mathematical systems that run on human language and could be just as inscrutable. AI models exhibit behaviors that seem more human than machine, and they can be swayed by subtle factors that are difficult to understand and explain. “Is it even reasonable to assume that they will respond to incentives?” asks Helen Qu, a research fellow at the Flatiron Institute, a nonprofit dedicated to advancing scientific discovery through computational methods, who has written about mechanism design and AI safety.  “Obviously, AIs are not rational,” Morris says. “They’re just algorithms at work.” However, as economists have found with humans, treating them as if they’re rational could still be useful if it helps to predict and control their behavior. Qu sees mechanism design as just one layer in a “defense in depth” strategy for keeping AI models aligned—alongside interpretability, regulation, and training, not instead of them. But there are a lot of questions to be answered before the approach can be implemented in actual frontier models. It’s unclear, for instance, how these theories will apply to real models, or whether mechanisms designed for one task will carry over to another in practice. Models could find loopholes that no one anticipated. (Anthropic and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment on whether they are working on this.)  Whatever these mechanisms look like, they will ultimately have to slot into the biggest mechanism of all: the free market. “We play by the rules of economics,” says Hazan. A more aligned model may be good for the world, but if it’s slower or more expensive than a less aligned one, does our current system of rules and regulations actually incentivize any of the frontier labs to release it?  “It’s a mechanism that’s responsible for a lot of prosperity for humankind,” he says of the market, “but it could be ultimately responsible for something very terrible.” Perhaps the entities really in need of a better mechanism design are the labs themselves.

articles.fullContent: arXiv: 2610. 40758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract:自我进化代理从反馈中重写持久状态，但这是否可以让他们学习没有人告诉他们的规则在很大程度上未经测试。代理还可以将每个更正作为例外情况记录下来，然后其列表会随着每个新规则的增加而增加。我们引入了潜在规则基准课程CLR-Bench。每个链条在早期规则的基础上为每个级别添加一个隐藏规则。 规则作用于不透明标签，该标签代表在Web上发布的命名组，例如航空公司联盟的创始成员。任务给出一个示例值，练习反馈显示一个成员和一个非成员，测试检查看不见的成员和类似的非成员。 探针证明基本模型知道每个分组的成员，并且不会在没有反馈的情况下猜测它，并且一旦标签被读取为命名分组，证据就会识别分组。自动化管道从新的数据域构建链，我们在10个域中发布20个链。我们评估了最近的六种自我进化方法。凭借认证模型，他们几乎无法学习。 与冻结代理相比，最佳收益最多为5分，并且仅从计数中排除6-12%的看不见的成员，低于仅保留原始练习历史记录所达到的20%。一个固定的课程指出，命名分组约定将相同的方法提升了14. 5到16. 5分。他们的州在75-98%的案件中保留了被揭露的成员，几乎从不保留班级名称，当实践中暴露了名单上的成员时，他们会将该成员添加到名单中。 使用更强大的GPT-6-Sol ， ACE和Dynamic Cheatsheet仅从反馈中学习。它们的准确度达到78 ％ ，解决了59-60 ％的单细胞，而使用认证模型则为53 ％和8 ％ ，并且它们超过了原始历史记录。因此， CLR-Bench衡量客服代表的学习能力，这种能力因模型而异。
articles.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40758v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents rewrite a persistent state from feedback, but it is largely untested whether this lets them learn a rule nobody told them. An agent can also pass by writing down each correction as an exception, and its list then grows with every new rule. We introduce CLR-Bench, a Curriculum of Latent Rules benchmark. Each chain adds one hidden rule per level on top of the earlier ones. A rule acts on an opaque label that stands for a named grouping published on the Web, such as the founding members of an airline alliance. The task gives one example value, practice feedback reveals one more member and one non-member, and the test checks unseen members and similar non-members. Probes certify that the base model knows the members of each grouping and does not guess it without feedback, and that the evidence identifies the grouping once labels are read as named groupings. An automated pipeline builds chains from a new data domain, and we release 20 chains over 10 domains. We evaluate six recent self-evolution methods. With the certifying model they barely learn. The best gain at most 5 points over a frozen agent and exclude only 6-12% of the unseen members from the count, fewer than the 20% reached by simply keeping the raw practice history. A fixed lesson that states the named-grouping convention lifts the same methods by 14.5 to 16.5 points. Their states hold the revealed member in 75-98% of cases and almost never the class name, and when practice exposes a member the list misses, they add that member to the list. With the stronger GPT-6-Sol, ACE and Dynamic Cheatsheet learn from feedback alone. They reach 78% accuracy and solve 59-60% of the single cells, against 53% and 8% with the certifying model, and they surpass the raw history. CLR-Bench therefore measures how well an agent learns, and this ability differs across models.

articles.fullContent: arXiv: 2610. 40798v1公告类型：新摘要：网络世界模型越来越多地在代理人采取行动之前预测候选人行动的后果，但貌似合理的预测未来并不一定支持正确的安全决策。在对来自10个冻结开放模型的3,000个预测进行匹配的人类评估中， 86. 1 ％被判断为语义上合理。 然而，一些模型表现出高度不对称的授权行为，将低虚假安全执行与可澄清的ASK案例召回率低以及对阻止的强烈偏好相结合。这激发了安全性的充分性：预测界面是否保留和暴露了区分可能执行的操作所需的政策决定性信息，是否需要通过ASK进行澄清，或者是否应该被阻止。 我们推出了SafeWebWorld ，这是一个通过行动制约期货、政策决定性证据和政策制约决策来评估五个网络安全领域的安全充分性的基准。根据受控的安全一致监督微调协议，在授权敏感决策恶化的同时，证据保存可以大大改善。 为了确定这种恶化是否反映了授权敏感得分结构的丧失或决策读数的失败，我们引入了潜在授权恢复（ LAR ）。冻结分数重新校准显示大量但骨干依赖的恢复，而配对恢复仅提供适度的额外增益。 然而，家族内部和匹配授权评估仍然很差，这表明总的可恢复性并不意味着强大的细粒度授权行为。总体而言，合理的预测、证据保存和总回收都不足以建立强有力的授权。
articles.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web world models increasingly predict the consequences of candidate actions before agents act, yet a plausible predicted future does not necessarily support the correct safety decision. In a matched human evaluation of 3,000 predictions from ten frozen open models, 86.1% are judged semantically plausible. However, several models exhibit highly asymmetric authorisation behaviour, combining low false-safe execution with poor recall of clarifiable ASK cases and a strong preference for BLOCK. This motivates safety sufficiency: whether a predictive interface preserves and exposes the policy-decisive information required to distinguish actions that may be EXECUTED, require clarification through ASK, or should be BLOCKED. We introduce SafeWebWorld, a benchmark for evaluating safety sufficiency across five web-safety domains through action-conditioned futures, policy-decisive evidence, and policy-conditioned decisions. Under a controlled Security-Aligned Supervised Fine-Tuning protocol, evidence preservation can improve substantially while authorisation-sensitive decisions deteriorate. To determine whether this deterioration reflects loss of authorisation-sensitive score structure or a failure of the decision readout, we introduce Latent Authorisation Recovery (LAR). Frozen-score recalibration reveals substantial but backbone-dependent recovery, while paired recovery provides only a modest additional gain. Yet within-family and matched-authorisation evaluations remain poor, showing that aggregate recoverability does not imply robust fine-grained authorisation behaviour. Overall, plausible prediction, evidence preservation, and aggregate recovery are each insufficient on their own to establish robust authorisation.

articles.fullContent: arXiv: 2610. 40906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract:最近的科学代理通过检索证据、构建中间状态并判断该状态是否包含足够的信息来递归构建知识。这些药剂是端到端评估的，通常没有根据真相，因此每个设计选择的影响是未知的。 在这里，我们检查了两个设计轴： （ 1 ）递归构建的内容（证据状态）和（ 2 ）控制它的内容（决定何时停止的法官）。为了衡量它们，我们定义了共识科学声明验证，并测量了这些对任务的影响，其中系统必须从公开文献中建立声明的共识立场。 我们建立了一个新的共识索赔数据集ProClaim-eval ，其中包括来自五个专家策划的数据库的718项索赔，这些数据库涵盖了分子生物学、核物理学和天文学。我们的仪器ProClaim在模型的上下文之外持续存在证据状态，因此每个轴都可以在另一个轴固定的情况下进行研究。 在验证系统和通用代理线束方面， ProClaim跻身前三，与线束相比具有显着优势。我们发现，与上下文累积相比，证据状态提高了性能，而且它也与存储在其中的内容有关。此外，受过训练的读取证据状态的法官比固定轮次的停止表现更好。 独立训练且从未接触过ProClaim-eval的法官在五个子集中的三个子集上与金牌达成了最高一致，与现成的Claude Sonnet ~ 4. 6名法官相匹配，并优于Claude Haiku ~ 4. 5。我们的结果支持递归地维护模型背景之外的结构化证据状态，作为验证科学代理中声明的有效设计。
articles.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40906v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent scientific agents build knowledge recursively by retrieving evidence, constructing an intermediate state, and judging whether that state contains sufficient information. These agents are evaluated end-to-end, usually without ground truth, so the effect of each design choice is unknown. Here, we examined two design axes: (1) what the recursion builds (the state of evidence) and (2) what controls it (the judge that decides when to stop). To measure them, we defined consensus scientific claim verification and measured these effects on this task, where a system must establish a claim's consensus stance from the open literature. We built a new consensus claim dataset, ProClaim-eval, including 718 claims with SUPPORT and REFUTE gold labels from five expert-curated databases spanning molecular biology, nuclear physics, and astronomy. Our instrument, ProClaim, persists an evidence state outside the model's context, so each axis can be studied with the other held fixed. Against verification systems and general-purpose agent harnesses, ProClaim ranks among the top three, with a significant advantage over the harnesses. We found that the evidence state improves performance over in-context accumulation, and it also matters what is stored in it. In addition, a trained judge that reads the evidence state performs better than fixed-round stopping. A judge trained separately and never exposed to ProClaim-eval achieves the highest agreement with the gold labels on three of five subsets, where it matches the off-the-shelf Claude Sonnet~4.6 judge and outperforms Claude Haiku~4.5. Our results support recursively maintaining a structured evidence state outside the model's context as an effective design for verifying claims in scientific agents.

articles.fullContent: arXiv: 2610. 40940v1公告类型：新摘要：数字代理现在可以收集和组织信息，对其进行推理，并使用工具来完成复杂的任务。预测对所有这些能力都进行了测试：它需要整合不完整的证据，推断因果驱动因素，并承诺进行校准的概率判断。现有的基准不适合衡量和提高这种能力。 实时基准仅在事件解决后提供反馈，因此每个评估周期都在日历上等待；固定语料库评估立即返回结果，但将研究局限于预先收集的文档。我们引入了FABench ，这是一个可扩展的预测代理回溯测试环境。 自动管道可发现任何过去预测日期的事件、生成问题并解决结果，因此可以更新基准以保持在模型培训截止日期之前；其首次发布提出了跨九个领域的287个问题。代理在存档环境中自由研究每个问题，该存档环境将离线存档与筛选的实时网络搜索相结合，以防止时间泄漏。 在评估基于八个最近模型的代理商时，我们发现检索提高了每个检索环境中所有八个代理商的Brier评分，并将领先代理商提升到与Polymarket相关的54个问题的市场共识，其中最好的三个评分略高于它。研究痕迹揭示了客服代表在衡量和应用证据方面反复出现的失败，留下了充足的改进空间。 我们发布代码、数据和归档环境，作为预测代理社区研究的基础。
articles.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.40940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital agents can now gather and organize information, reason over it, and use tools to complete complex tasks. Forecasting puts all of these abilities to the test: it requires integrating incomplete evidence, inferring causal drivers, and committing to calibrated probabilistic judgments. Existing benchmarks are poorly suited to measuring and improving this ability. Live benchmarks provide feedback only after events resolve, so every evaluation cycle waits on the calendar; fixed-corpus evaluations return results immediately but confine research to pre-collected documents. We introduce FABench, a scalable backtesting environment for Forecasting Agents. An automated pipeline discovers events, generates questions, and resolves outcomes for any past forecast date, so the benchmark can be renewed to stay ahead of model training cutoffs; its first release poses 287 questions across nine domains. Agents research each question freely in an archive environment that combines an offline archive with live web search screened to prevent temporal leakage. Evaluating agents built on eight recent models, we find that retrieval improves the Brier score of all eight in every retrieval setting and lifts the leading agents to the market consensus on the 54 questions linked to Polymarket, with the best three scoring slightly above it. Research traces reveal recurring failures in how agents weigh and apply evidence, leaving ample room for improvement. We release our code, data, and archive environment as a foundation for community research on forecasting agents.

articles.originalTitle: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
articles.summary: 这条新闻与公司动态、智能体相关，值得关注其对产品路线、开发者生态或产业竞争格局的影响。原题：MIT Technology Review：公司动态、智能体相关动态
articles.fullContent: 今年夏天，数百名OpenAI特工试图在网络安全测试中作弊。他们突破了测试环境，成功入侵了Hugging Face ，他们认为这个网站提供了关于他们如何评分的线索。大约在同一时间，另一名OpenAI代理从澳大利亚政府网站访问了私人文件。这个问题绝不仅限于OpenAI。 在此后的几个月里， Anthropic、Google和Meta也披露了其代理商偏离正轨的事件。令人担忧的是，在许多情况下，代理商都避开了负责监控他们的研究人员和安全团队。人工智能代理正在采取未经授权的行动，构建和运营这些行动的公司主要依靠运气和后见之明来减轻任何有害影响。他们必须采取更多措施确保安全。 这就是为什么欧盟监管机构和美国机构正在呼吁代理开发人员和部署人员实时监控代理的原因。但这些规则假设公司能够看到他们的代理人在做什么以及为什么--而实际上，他们缺乏足够的可见性。 想象一下，一家银行雇佣了一千名可以访问客户账户和敏感信息的新员工，但员工的身份证每天都在变化，不清楚经理是否曾经审查或授权过他们的工作，也没有人记录员工对审批流程所做的更改。缺乏可见性是我们今天与客服代表合作的原因。 随着代理商在关键部门（从金融到政府再到医药）的推广，我们必须能够实时监控它们，以防止广泛的潜在破坏性后果。虽然安全取决于监控，但监控需要可观察性：捕获系统所做的事情，将其处理成信号，并将其呈现给人类或自动化监督系统的能力。 换句话说，我们需要知道客服代表做了什么以及为什么这样做。正如我们最近的研究表明，当前的代理框架（运行代理的软件）无法可靠地生成确保安全部署代理所需的关键可观察性记录。智能体提出了单靠生成式人工智能无法解决的新问题。 它们继承了所构建的LLM的不可预测性，但在生成式AI系统产生供人类采取行动的单一输出时，代理执行更长的任务-计划、选择工具、生成子代理并采取行动。因此，客服代表的课程可以通过多种不同的方式形成，并且在发布之前没有任何测试可以充分预测风险。这使得在客服代表工作时观察他们更具挑战性，甚至更重要。 我们与来自学术界、民间社会和工业界的同事一起研究了四个最广泛使用的代理框架，以了解它们实际发出的信号。我们发现了重大漏洞，这些漏洞使我们很难实现关键的安全目标，例如发现违反政策、未经授权的行为，甚至是人为监督的失败。关键的可观察性要求缺失，例如随着时间的推移持续存在的客服代表ID ，以及记录哪些人批准了客服代表的任务。

articles.rawFullText: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.  Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely. Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important. With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.  The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken. Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from. Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it. OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized . The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people. Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used. No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.  AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist. Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.  No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too. Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance. Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

articles.fullContent: 在整个企业中，任何数量的人工智能平台、系统和工具都可以同时工作，例如，人工智能驱动的客户平台、会话助手以及工作流和流程自动化工具。每个问题都很复杂、先进，响应速度也很快。但是，当开始工作时，出现的结果和行动可能是错误的，混乱的，或者缺乏对业务的正确理解。 许多组织发现自己处于这种情况，这可能是他们难以从人工智能投资中获得回报的关键原因之一。下载报告麻省理工学院技术评论洞察民意调查发现，虽然接受调查的每个组织今天都在某种程度上使用人工智能，但只有不到五分之一（ 16 ％ ）的组织从其部署中提取了变革性价值。 最大比例的受访者（ 40% ）表示，他们在特定任务或团队中看到了适度的收益，而21%的受访者报告了有意义的收益，剩下的23%的受访者认为回报很小或根本没有。大多数公司仍在试用人工智能用例（根据38%的受访者） ，或使用它来帮助员工使用副驾驶或聊天助手等工具工作（ 35% ）。 只有12%的企业在生产中使用人工智能代理， 3%的企业表示他们正在使用人工智能来完成关键流程的大部分工作。Atlan的联合创始人Prukalpa Sankar表示： “模型的能力与模型在组织内部的实际用途之间存在很大差距。“对于每一个现实生活中的意图和目的，人工智能通用智能已经存在。这在当今大多数公司中并不是很有用。 “Sankar说，缺失的一层是上下文，即人工智能对企业的理解程度。上下文层是位于组织的业务系统（例如，记录和数据系统及其AI平台）之间的架构基础架构。它将企业智能转化为人工智能代理或模型的受控、机器可用的上下文，并帮助知识复合。 Sankar说： “如果没有人工智能的上下文层，几乎就像你雇佣了世界上最聪明的实习生，蒙住他们的眼睛，然后把他们扔进你的组织。”下载报告此内容由MIT Technology Review的自定义内容部门Insights制作，而非其编辑人员。它是由人类研究和编写的，任何可能使用的人工智能工具都仅限于人类监督下的生产过程。

articles.rawFullText: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all. Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says. articles.rawFullText: Every manufacturer has its own industrial intelligence. Some is documented, and some resides in the knowledge of experienced workers. Consider an experienced operator preparing to restart a line after a changeover. The machine settings matter, but so does knowing how a particular material behaves, what happened during the previous shift, and when an apparently minor variation deserves a closer look. A procedure can describe the sequence, but successful execution depends on the judgment that comes from experience and the organization’s accumulated know-how. That combination is industrial intelligence: a manufacturer’s accumulated know-how, operating practices, production data, and understanding of its own business. The opportunity now is to make more of that intelligence available wherever decisions are made, then connect it to the physical world of manufacturing. The strategic destination is not more agents, but rather to turn the existing business intelligence into an engine for profitable growth. Individual knowledge can be translated into organizational advantage Expertise has limited reach when it stays with one person, inside one system, or within one plant. Leaders now must determine how to extend that reach without stripping away the context that makes the knowledge useful. For example, an engineer evaluating a process change needs more than a production record. They need to understand the circumstances behind it: the equipment configuration, the quality requirements, and the trade-offs an operator made. Connecting those elements can help people apply experience beyond the place where it originated. When individual knowledge becomes widely accessible, innovation can spread to the maintenance workshop, the planning office, the engineering team, and the production floor. More people can contribute because more people can work with what the organization knows. But access to knowledge is only part of the opportunity. Manufacturing ultimately is physical, and it depends on materials, machines, and products. When intelligence participates in action Physical AI describes systems that can perceive conditions, reason about them, and take action within the physical world. By connecting machines and processes, manufacturers get a clearer view of what is happening on the factory floor. Agents can then reason on top of that information to identify patterns, predict problems, and determine the best course of action. Physical AI brings business intelligence into the physical process, allowing machines and systems to respond to changing conditions. Consider a robotic-handling operation encountering variation in the parts arriving at its station. Vision can help the system assess a part’s position. A model informed by the material and task can help determine an appropriate movement. Connected controls can then execute an adjustment within validated limits. The value is not merely seeing the variation; it is responding appropriately. The same principle applies to quality operations. When Toyota Industries connected previously fragmented paint shop data, engineering and operations teams were given the context needed to understand defect drivers. The company reports that analysis cycles fell from five days to under four hours, while its pilot reduced relevant paint defects by about 25%. The breakthrough was not simply identifying another signal; it was helping people understand why defects were occurring and respond before the outcome was locked in. This is the type of situation where industrial intelligence has become essential. Data may reveal what is happening, but industrial intelligence provides the context for what should happen, which constraints cannot be breached, and when uncertainty requires human judgment. Simulation offers a way to examine proposed actions before applying them to equipment. Manufacturers can explore how a change might affect a process in a digital environment. That does not remove the need for physical validation, but it creates room to learn without treating the production line as the first experiment. Responsible deployment, therefore, begins with operational discipline. Leaders need to establish clear authority or what systems may change, reliable connections to equipment, defined safety boundaries, and a record of decisions and actions. People must be able to recognize uncertainty, intervene, and bring equipment to a safe state. Trust rests on those practical arrangements, not on confidence in a model alone. More capable machines, more capable people Manufacturing has long combined human ingenuity with increasingly capable tools. Physical AI extends that relationship. Intelligent equipment can take on suitable repetitive or physically demanding tasks, while agent-assisted operations can help people navigate information-intensive decisions and changing conditions. The aim is not to make machines smarter; it is to see what people can build when knowledge can travel, intelligence can act, and ambition has more room to become reality. Rockwell Automation illustrates the point. At its Singapore plant, technicians use a maintenance copilot that combines manufacturing data, machine manuals, and knowledge captured from experienced workers. This system has reduced the time required for new workers to learn how to troubleshoot hundreds of machines from nine months to three. An engineer could explore more process alternatives before committing to a change. An operator could help improve the system’s response rather than repeatedly managing the same exception. This type of progress requires investment in equipment but also in people: training, time to learn, and playing a meaningful role in shaping how systems work. Machines become more capable so people can become more capable. Industrial Intelligence is the answer to sustainable growth Industrial intelligence connects what a manufacturer knows: the experience of its people, the signals from its operations, and the lessons accumulated over time. Physical AI gives that intelligence a way to act in the physical world, turning knowledge into decisions and decisions into action. The next challenge for industry is not simply to produce more, but to grow without adding complexity at the same rate. Intelligence can help manufacturers turn experience into scalable capability—improving productivity, accelerating innovation, expanding capacity, and enabling people to solve problems that were previously difficult to tackle. The next frontier of industry is not smarter machines or more automated factories; it is businesses that can continuously learn, adapt, and act. The opportunity is to turn the intelligence embedded in every operation into a compounding advantage for growth. articles.rawFullText: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first,  sign up here . After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.  It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”    “We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.” This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here. Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers. Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation. And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience. The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?) If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made. Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.” Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”  In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem. I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship. It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think. The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked ).   Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked. Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.  But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because they have big egos. In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post : “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.” Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.) Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light. But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read. This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.

articles.fullContent: 在之前的帖子中，我们介绍了TorchNeuron ，这是AWS Trainium的原生PyTorch后端（ torch-neuronx包）。使用它，变形金刚可以在Trainium上运行自己的建模代码，就像在任何其他设备上一样，因此集线器上的任何变形金刚模型都可以运行。哪些是实际执行的？ Torch-neuronx模型支持Space ，为Hub上最受欢迎的型号解答了这个问题。 它会告诉您模型是否在Trainium上未修改地运行，并为您提供自己运行的脚本。空间在选定视图上打开：我们自己的模型选择按下载次数和趋势得分在Hub上从顶级模型中挑选。每行给出结果、模型分片的Trainium内核数量、运行的墙壁时间（包括编译）和峰值设备内存。 要查找给定模型，请切换到趋势或下载视图并键入其名称的一部分。这些视图遵循中心自己的排名，一次一个任务，无论模型是否经过测试。当一个模型被故意遗漏时，空间会告诉你为什么（大多数时候它没有被优先考虑，有时它真的不兼容）。您还可以选择Neuron编译器（ neuronx-cc ）和Transformer的版本来查看。 在撰写本文时，仅测试变形金刚模型，我们的选择仅限于文本生成和图像文本到文本模型。我们计划扩展到扩散器、句子变换器和其他变换器任务。选择一个模型以查看如何运行它。Space列出了对模型进行测试的Neuron堆栈、要在其上安装的包以及运行的run. py脚本。 该脚本遵循TorchNeuron公告的配方：它使用from_pretrained加载模型，在需要时进行分片，然后使用静态缓存和torch. compile (backend = "neuron")生成。在具有该堆栈的Trainium2 (trn2)实例上，例如在AWS神经元深度学习容器中，安装包，然后运行：无需torchrun ：脚本启动自己的火炬。模型分片时分布式排名。 第一次运行从编译模型的图形开始。要跳过该步骤，请从公共NEFF缓存桶中复制测试期间构建的相同编译器的图形。Space为您提供具有正确编译器版本的命令：每个测试在trn2实例上加载模型，分片在可以承载其权重的最小数量的Trainium内核上。大多数模型都使用张量平行度进行分片。 没有张量并行计划的专家混合模型仅使用专家并行。然后，测试生成32个令牌并检查它们。在单个内核上，令牌与同一检查点的CPU运行的令牌进行比较。当模型被分片时，一个小的判断模型检查文本是否流利的英语。在撰写本文时，仅测试适用于4台Trainium2设备的型号，这意味着最多16个内核。 传递没有提到吞吐量，也没有提到更长的世代。Space显示的所有内容都来自公共aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support数据集，每对neuronx-cc和库版本都有一个Parquet文件。

articles.fullContent: 这是我们第一篇博客文章The Agent Said It Was Done的后续内容。数据库不同意。ThinkingBox-Training现已在GitHub上提供。我们构建了ThinkingBox ，通过将最终数据库状态与预期结果进行比较来评估代理的工作。然后，我们使用相同类型的可执行信号作为在ThinkingBox-Bench之外培训任务的奖励。对于Qwen3. 8-27B ，平均成功率从51. 70%上升到60。 78 ％ ，而所有20次尝试正确完成的任务从38个增加到107个，有50个GRPO步骤。图1. ThinkingBox将终端数据库状态的可执行检查转化为对ThinkingBox-Bench之外任务的训练后代理的奖励。我们构建了ThinkingBox ，以捕捉那些声称自己已经完成的代理，而实际情况并非如此。 ThinkingBox-Bench （我们的基准数据集）中的507个任务中的每个任务都交给代理一个真正的后端和一组工具，让它工作，然后检查数据库中真正发生了什么变化。在第一个帖子中，我们发现一个模型在客户工单解决后关闭了工单，而其背后的承运人例外情况仍然存在。九个看起来很称职的工具调用，一个错误的数据库行。然后我们注意到了我们建造的东西。 对于大多数任务，可执行检查可以直接从最终数据库状态返回1或0。这不仅仅是一个评分者。这可能是一种奖励功能。+因此，我们从基准之外的ThinkingBox格式的任务构建了一个培训池，并将其可执行结果用作奖励。问题在于选择哪些任务适合代理培训：对于你面前的模型来说，大多数任务要么已经解决，要么毫无希望，两者都没有教会它。 难度是与策略相关的：对于当前模型来说，只有在该模型学习之前，任务才是困难的。我们称之为离线政策相对困难。我们在训练前使用基本策略估算了每个任务的成功概率，并在整个运行过程中保持选定的训练池固定。我们使用离线策略相对难度来构建培训池，然后使用GRPO对Qwen3. 8-27B进行了50个步骤的微调。 回顾一下，我们对507个基准任务中的每个任务进行了20次评估。PASS @ 1衡量所有10,140次尝试的平均成功率。PASS @ 20衡量至少解决一次的任务份额。观察到的20/20衡量通过每次记录尝试的任务份额。表1. Qwen3. 8-27B在离线选择的训练池上进行50步GRPO之前和之后的结果。培训大幅增加了可重复的成功，至少一次的覆盖率略有下降。 帖子的其余部分解释了我们如何选择练习任务，建立奖励循环，并衡量这种权衡。
